q1.answer: No: ADR013 (node-fetch) is superseded and no longer applies. It was replaced by ADR014, which says frontend plugins and packages should prefer the fetchApiRef (injected via useApi), while Node.js code should use the native fetch; this matches NotificationsClient.ts taking an injected fetchApi rather than importing an HTTP library.

q2.answer: ADR007 requires using msw with express-style route handlers for any fetch/XMLHttpRequest mocking in tests. It says this avoids each test having its own, inconsistent implementation of mocking network requests, and avoids the pain/duplication of writing bespoke mocking code per test.

q3.answer: ADR006 says React.FC/React.SFC implicitly add a children prop, and do not support generic types on children. It also notes that Facebook removed React.FC from the create-react-app TypeScript base template (via PR #8177) because it was deemed unnecessary with mostly downsides.

q4.answer: The replaced library is Moment.js. ADR010 gives two reasons it's being retired: it has large bundle sizes and mutable-state issues, and the Moment.js project itself is being sunset and recommends switching to a more modern alternative.

q5.answer: ADR004 (Module Export Structure) requires every exported symbol to be traceable through index files down to src/index.ts. It was written to make it easy to answer 'is this export in this module also exported by the package (or directory)?' — i.e., determining a module's public API boundary.

q6.answer: No, per ADR004's rule they are not part of the public API: since there is no src/utils/index.ts re-exporting them and src/index.ts doesn't mention them, the chain of index-file re-exports up to the package root is broken, so by the rule's own logic (traceability through index files is required to count as exported) these files are implicitly private even without any explicit 'private' marker.

q7.answer: ADR011 defines x-react as containing shared widgets, hooks and similar code that both the plugin itself and third-party frontend plugins can depend on; a -react package is only justified once other, third-party frontend plugins actually need to depend on notifications' components/hooks. For plugins/notifications to need one, some of its components/hooks would have to become reusable building blocks that other plugins want to import directly.

q8.answer: The one exception ADR003 allows is React.lazy modules, since React.lazy requires a default export. The workaround it gives is to keep named exports and adapt them at the import site, e.g. `React.lazy(() => import('../path/to/Component').then(m => ({ default: m.Component })))`.

q9.answer: That pattern is defined in ADR015. Its Consequences section explicitly says the team will update APIs for the new frontend system (@backstage/frontend-* packages) but will not update any existing APIs for the old frontend system in the @backstage/core-* packages — i.e. pre-existing dev-app-style code like dev/index.tsx won't be retrofitted.
